question.problem: If ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14117453/assets/0009074502b2f719bcc6c4ba4726e93a3c75386be4e7f9c19a8a33336f8c7fba.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14117453/assets/8774988415a7fdb8bd16aa2bd2ccd03a7e94ffd272b23a11bc2f561d855f2e8a.svg) are solutions to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ find $A\mathbf{w}(t)$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14117453/assets/5712d4375732622b9bd533e98d61ba41e0057c88b9daf0e48d12ef9c9465e3d8.svg)
question.worked_solution:
Since $\mathbf{u}(t)$ and $\mathbf{v}(t)$ are solutions to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ the superposition principle guarantees that 

$$
c\mathbf{u}(t) + d\mathbf{v}(t)
$$

 is also a solution to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)$ for all $c,d\in\mathbb{R}.$

Notice that 

$$
\mathbf{w}(t)=4\mathbf{u}(t)+6\mathbf{v}(t).
$$

 

Therefore, $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t).$ So, in order to find $A\mathbf{w}(t)$ we just need to find $\mathbf{w}'(t)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Aw & ={w}^{′}(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(4{e}^{4t})^{′} \\ (6{e}^{5t})^{′}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16{e}^{4t} \\ 30{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
